Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Start time: 15:42 PST
Duration: 52 mins (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Sabrina Lowe (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Head of ML, Oxbridge), Marco Ruiz (Platform Eng), Priya Desai (Security), Tom Evers (CTO)

Auto summary (auto-generated):

- Key constraints: SOC2 + internal audit, KMS/HSM for keys, VPC peering, data residency for EU workloads, burst-to-hosted fallback strategy.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 50 minutes, quick intros, then Ravi will do a bit on topology and warm-pool and then we'll go into compliance questions. Lena, do you want to start with a quick intro to your goals?
[00:18] Lena Ortiz: Yeah thanks Maya. So, Oxbridge is building a realtime recommendations API that needs ~20ms p95 for short prompts, and we do a mix of short and long generation. We're evaluating whether we go Redwood hosted or take Dedicated to get isolation and predictable latency.
[00:33] Tom Evers: We also have an internal audit—so logs, key control, and encryption at rest are must-haves.
[00:40] Maya Chen: Totally, that'll frame things. Ravi, want to kick off with how Dedicated pools look?
[00:45] Ravi Patel: Sure. So the way we do Dedicated is reserved GPU pools —you get a set of nodes reserved to your account. We support hot-pool prewarm (we call warm-pools internally), and policies for burst into shared-hosted if you want overflow capacity. The warm-pool keeps models loaded and KV cache warm which is important for that tail latency.
[01:10] Marco Ruiz: Quick question—if we reserve say 8 nodes, can we segment them? We have two product teams that need logical isolation.
[01:20] Ravi Patel: Yes, you can do tenant fencing inside your reserved capacity with node-level segmentation, or dedicate pools per team. There's also process-level RBAC. One tradeoff is utilization—you'll pay for reservation but you control tenancy.
[01:36] Lena Ortiz: What's the expected cold-start if we don't keep warm-pool? Our peak is spiky — short bursts every 5 minutes.
[01:44] Ravi Patel: Cold-start can be hundreds of ms to a few seconds depending on model size and quantization. With warm-pool prewarm and KV cache persistence, we typically keep p95 within your 20-40ms target for small seqs. For larger sequences it grows.
[02:05] Priya Desai: On encryption—we need to know KMS and HSM options. We can't have keys outside our control for sensitive features.
[02:13] Maya Chen: Understood. We support customer-managed KMS in Private deployments and for Dedicated we have KMS integrations with major cloud KMS and can discuss HSM-backed key storage via an enterprise plan. Sabrina, anything to add?
[02:26] Sabrina Lowe: I'll add that audit logs include token-level request metadata and model traces, depending on retention tier. We can push logs to your SIEM via S3 or a streaming connector.
[02:38] Marco Ruiz: If we do VPC peering, how does traffic flow? Do we have egress through our VPC or Redwood handles the egress?
[02:46] Ravi Patel: For Dedicated inside Private VPC, traffic stays inside your VPC and you manage routing. For Redwood-hosted Dedicated, we can set up VPC peering/PrivateLink so data path is private. There is a small NAT/Egress consideration for metrics and control-plane calls, we can document that.
[03:04] Lena Ortiz: Let's talk burst: We don't want to over-provision but need to survive 10x sudden traffic. What's your recommended approach?
[03:12] Ravi Patel: Two patterns: 1) Reserved + warm-pool sized for typical peak and burst into hosted via policy-based overflow for occasional spikes. 2) Reserved sized for baseline and autoscale with pre-configured burst capacity that uses queued requests and can degrade quality—e.g. quantized model variant for overflow. Both have cost/latency tradeoffs.
[03:35] Tom Evers: Overflow to hosted worries us for data residency. Some of our calls must stay in EU.
[03:41] Maya Chen: Good point. We can implement region-aware fallback—if the EU region is your compliance boundary, we can fallback only to EU-hosted nodes or refuse fallback and instead queue/return 429s. That choice is policy-driven.
[03:57] Priya Desai: For SOC2 evidence, do you have a SOC2 Type II? And do you give encryption key rotation logs?
[04:05] Sabrina Lowe: Yes we publish SOC2 Type II for the platform. For key rotation, if you're on a customer-managed KMS, rotations are in your control and we ingest rotation metadata into audit logs. If using Redwood-managed KMS we have rotation logs we can include in the compliance pack.
[04:21] Marco Ruiz: Let's be practical—what's the typical latency overhead of warm-pool vs cold start on an Llama-style 13B?
[04:28] Ravi Patel: For 13B-ish, cold start cross seconds, warm-pool gets you down to tens of ms for short prompts. There are variables—quant, sequence length, kv cache hit ratio. We ran internal tests with 13B quantized where p50 ~ 12ms p95 ~ 38ms for 64-token workloads on our optimized kernels. Your mileage will vary.
[04:49] Lena Ortiz: That's promising. Marco: our peak QPS during campaigns hits 240 qps briefly—can Redwood handle that with reserved nodes?
[04:57] Ravi Patel: Depends on your model and batch sizing. For 240 qps at 20ms p95 you need enough concurrency and batching strategy. We typically model tokens-per-second per-GPU and come up with node counts; we'll need your traces.
[05:12] Tom Evers: On SLA—what uptime and latency SLOs do you offer for Dedicated?
[05:18] Maya Chen: Dedicated comes with stronger SLAs—uptime SLA is enterprise-tiered and latency SLOs can be negotiated in reserved contracts, especially with warm-pool guarantees. We'll put exact numbers in the contract.
[05:30] Priya Desai: Any multi-tenant noisy neighbor protections? We can't have other customers impacting our p95.
[05:36] Ravi Patel: Dedicated is physically reserved, so noisy neighbors at the Redwood-hosted side won't co-locate on those GPUs. Within your reserved pool, we offer cgroup-level isolation if you share nodes between teams.
[05:48] Lena Ortiz: For burst to hosted—if we choose to overflow, how do you sanitize logs and ensure PII isn't sent outside control?
[05:58] Sabrina Lowe: We can implement request-level redaction rules or route only anonymized or metadata-only requests for overflow. That requires engineering tradeoffs. We usually recommend sensitive workloads keep within Private deployments.
[06:12] Marco Ruiz: How does autoscaling decision making work on Dedicated? Is it reactive or predictive?
[06:20] Ravi Patel: We support both. You can configure CPU/GPU metrics thresholds and a predictive ramp-up based on time-series patterns. For very spiky workloads we recommend predictive prewarm windows tied to traffic signals from your side.
[06:34] Tom Evers: Our SREs want to test failover. Can we do a tabletop exercise?
[06:39] Maya Chen: Absolutely, we run failover drills with customers. We can script a simulated outage and demonstrate fallback to hosted or queue behavior.
[06:47] Lena Ortiz: A couple more technical points—does Redwood support persistent KV cache across restarts?
[06:53] Ravi Patel: KV cache can be persisted to local NVMe-backed storage in Dedicated to speed cold-restart recovery. There's a durability vs cost choice.
[07:05] Marco Ruiz: If we use quantized variants for overflow, do we get deterministic output changes? We need to know quality delta.
[07:12] Sabrina Lowe: Quantized variants can differ; we recommend evaluating with your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and run regressions against your eval sets.
[07:24] [00:07:30] Lena Ortiz: (overlap) Can you run a bias/regression eval as part of the pilot?
[07:29] Ravi Patel: Yes, we can run your eval harness in the benchmark window and produce quality/regression reports.
[07:35] [00:07:40] Marco Ruiz: Network egress—if we peer via PrivateLink, what about control-plane telemetry back to Redwood?
[07:44] Maya Chen: Minimal control-plane calls go out for orchestration, but metrics and logs can be pushed to your collector instead of Redwood. We'll document exact ports and endpoints.
[07:55] Priya Desai: We'd like to see a sample of the audit log schema.
[07:59] Sabrina Lowe: I'll attach the schema in the follow-up. It includes request id, model id, token counts, user id (optional), and the key-handling reference.
[08:09] [00:08:20] Tom Evers: What's the onboarding timeline—if we sign next quarter, how fast can you provision a dedicated pool?
[08:17] Maya Chen: For standard reserved pools, provisioning is generally 2-4 weeks depending on region and hardware availability. Private on-prem is longer.
[08:26] Marco Ruiz: During that provisioning window can we run canary tests on hosted to validate prompts?
[08:31] Maya Chen: Yes, many customers start on hosted and then transition to Dedicated. We'll map model versions to ensure parity.
[08:40] [00:08:50] Lena Ortiz: Regarding costs, do you have a formula for warm-pool charges vs active usage?
[08:47] Maya Chen: Warm-pools carry a lower baseline cost than fully active GPUs but you pay for reserved capacity. We bill a reservation fee plus usage when active; we'll share a spreadsheet.
[08:57] Marco Ruiz: Any special considerations for GPU preemption? If we get preempted in cloud infra, do you migrate workloads?
[09:04] Ravi Patel: In Dedicated we try to use non-preemptible instances for predictable latency; if using spot for cost-savings, we provide graceful eviction handlers and migration policies.
[09:13] [00:09:20] Priya Desai: Can you support customer-managed HSM for keys used to encrypt request payloads?
[09:20] Sabrina Lowe: We can integrate with external HSM via KMIP or cloud HSM interfaces under enterprise contracts—there's an onboarding checklist but yes.
[09:31] Marco Ruiz: For the benchmark run, what's a realistic test harness? We want to include ramp, steady, and spike phases.
[09:38] Ravi Patel: We usually do a 2-hour window: 30m warm-up, 60m steady-state at baseline QPS, 30m spike series with 5-10x bursts. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and tail jitter.
[09:51] Lena Ortiz: Ok that works. Marco will provide traces and we'll schedule benchmark next week.
[09:57] Maya Chen: Great. Pivoting—Priya, any legal/compliance showstoppers you foresee?
[10:03] Priya Desai: Not showstoppers yet, but we need clear audit trail for key access and proof of encryption in transit and at rest. Also SSO/SAML integration for RBAC.
[10:12] Maya Chen: We support SAML/SCIM for user provisioning and RBAC. Key access events are logged. We'll share sample logs.
[10:21] [00:10:30] Tom Evers: One more on model pinning—if we pin a model version, can Redwood do canary rollouts inside our reserved pool?
[10:30] Ravi Patel: Yes. We support canary and A/B within Dedicated with traffic-splitting policies and automatic rollback rules.
[10:38] Marco Ruiz: Regarding telemetry retention—how long do you retain request-level logs?
[10:44] Sabrina Lowe: Default short retention, but enterprise packages allow extended retention for logs and traces. We'll include retention tiers in the follow-up.
[10:53] Lena Ortiz: For the pilot, we want to validate quality delta between 13B full-fp and 13B quantized overflow. Can Redwood run paralleled runs to compare?
[11:02] Ravi Patel: Yes, we can run side-by-side comparisons during the benchmark window and produce regression reports.
[11:08] [00:11:15] Maya Chen: Great. Quick note—Anthropic was mentioned earlier. Do you want an overview of how we differ?
[11:20] Tom Evers: Mainly about dedicated isolation and warm-pool economics—others offer endpoints but not this granularity.
[11:27] Maya Chen: Understood. Last: let's recap next steps.
[11:31] Ravi Patel: I'll prepare the benchmark runbook and recommended starting topology—probably two warm-pool nodes per team then scale.
[11:40] Maya Chen: I'll send pricing spreadsheet, SOC2 + KMS docs, and the benchmark schedule invite. Sabrina will attach audit log schema.
[11:48] Marco Ruiz: We'll share traces and schedule the SRE deep-dive.
[11:52] Priya Desai: We'll review the compliance docs and revert.
[11:56] Maya Chen: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email and create the benchmark ticket in your CRM.
[12:03] Tom Evers: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
